title: Full-response SSRF in workflow api_call action node (no URL validation, redirects followed)
description: The workflow engine's api_call action node fetches an arbitrary attacker-supplied URL with no scheme, host, or IP validation, and returns the full response body to the caller. The fetch client follows redirects, allowing allowlist-free pivoting to loopback/link-internal targets. A related sink exists in the MCP server "test connection" endpoint, which HEADs an attacker-registered host_address with no validation (blind).
impact: An authenticated low-privilege user who can create/edit a workflow (api_call node) makes the backend issue requests to arbitrary internal addresses (loopback, RFC1918, link-local/cloud metadata) and reads the full response body back through workflow execution results/logs — full (non-blind) SSRF. Redirect-following defeats any future allowlist unless re-validated per hop.
technical_analysis: Root cause: `ActionNodeExecutor.executeApiCall` (super-agent/backend/src/services/node-executors/action-executor.ts:114-162) takes `apiConfig.url` from the workflow node's `data.metadata` (line 117-118: `metadata?.apiConfig`), substitutes variables, and passes it directly to `fetch()` (line 137) with no URL validation whatsoever. The parsed response body is placed into the success result (`response: parsedResponse`, line 157), which flows into workflow execution records/logs visible to the caller. Node's global `fetch` follows redirects by default, so an attacker-controlled external URL can 302 to `http://169.254.169.254/...` or any internal host. Reachability: workflow nodes (including `metadata` with `apiConfig`) are supplied via `POST /api/workflows` (routes/workflows.routes.ts:275, `authenticate + requireModifyAccess`, `nodes: {type:'array'}` with no per-node schema) and executed via `POST /api/workflows/:id/execute-v2` (line 967, `authenticate`), via the public unauthenticated webhook trigger path (webhook.service.ts executeWebhookAsync builds the same plan and runs workflowExecutorV2), and via workflow-execution.service.ts:1027 (nodeExecutorRegistry.execute). A duplicate sink exists in `WorkflowOrchestrator.executeActionNode` (services/workflow-orchestrator.ts:536-565) with the same unvalidated `fetch(url, ...)` at line 554 and response returned at line 567. Additional sink: `McpServerService.testMcpServerConnection` (services/mcp.service.ts:245-248) fetches `config.url || server.host_address` (user-registered via POST /api/mcp/servers, authenticated) with attacker-controlled headers — blind SSRF (only status/latency/error returned).
poc_description: 1. Start a mock "internal" HTTP server on 127.0.0.1:47777 returning a secret, and a redirector on 127.0.0.1:46666 that 302s to it. 2. Instantiate ActionNodeExecutor and execute a node with data.metadata.actionType='api_call' and apiConfig.url='http://127.0.0.1:46666/'. 3. Observe the node result's output contains the internal server's body, proving redirect-following SSRF with full response disclosure. Repeat with the internal URL directly.
remediation_steps: Introduce a shared SSRF guard for all outbound URL fetches driven by user input: validate scheme (https/http only), resolve DNS and reject loopback, RFC1918, link-local (169.254/16, metadata ranges), and IPv6-mapped variants; use `redirect: 'manual'` and re-validate each hop before following (or disable redirects entirely); cap response size. Apply the guard in the workflow api_call executors, the MCP test-connection path, and any future outbound fetch of user-supplied URLs.
evidence: Local PoC (tsx against the real executor, loopback-only): mock internal server on 127.0.0.1:47777 returned `SECRET-INTERNAL-DATA`; a redirector on 127.0.0.1:46666 answered with `302 -> http://127.0.0.1:47777/`. Executing an api_call node with url `http://127.0.0.1:46666/` produced a success result whose output contained `SECRET-INTERNAL-DATA` — i.e. the client followed the redirect to the internal address and returned the body. Direct loopback URL (`http://127.0.0.1:47777/`) likewise returned the body. Source trace: `executeApiCall` calls `fetch(url, ...)` (action-executor.ts:137) with `url` from `apiConfig.url` (line 117), then returns `response: parsedResponse` (line 157). No validation anywhere between route input and sink.
assumptions: Assumes an authenticated user who can create or edit workflows (api_call action nodes) or an MCP server — both are standard low-priv tenant capabilities behind `authenticate`.
counterevidence: Checked: no URL validation, allowlist, scheme check, IP/host restriction, or redirect handling exists in either executor path (action-executor.ts executeApiCall, workflow-orchestrator.ts executeActionNode). Node `nodes`/`metadata` accepted without schema validation in workflow create/execute routes. The only nearby control is org-scoped workflow lookup (workflowRepository.findById with organizationId), which gates who may run the workflow but never inspects the URL. Impact limited to internal network read (response is returned to caller); no write primitive demonstrated.
severity_change_conditions: Confirmation that the deployed backend can reach cloud metadata or internal admin services from the fetch sink would confirm network-level impact; conversely an egress-blocking network policy at deployment would reduce severity.

title: Unauthenticated generic IM webhook allows arbitrary agent message injection and workflow triggering
description: The generic IM webhook endpoint `POST /api/im/webhook/:bindingId` performs no authentication, signature verification, or replay protection. Any network caller who knows a binding UUID can inject arbitrary text into the agent chat pipeline, trigger agent execution, and create chat sessions.
impact: Unauthenticated remote attacker can drive the platform's AI agents with arbitrary prompts under a tenant's identity: create chat sessions (confirmed), inject persistent user messages, trigger agent/LLM execution and downstream agent actions, and consume tenant quota.
technical_analysis: src/routes/im.routes.ts:733-764 registers POST /webhook/:bindingId with no authenticate preHandler and never calls verifyAndLookupBinding or any adapter verifyRequest. It looks the binding up by ID alone (findBindingById, im.routes.ts:767-771, explicitly "without org context") and builds a NormalizedIMMessage from attacker-supplied text/user_id/thread_id, flowing into imService.handleMessage (im.service.ts:171) → session creation, message persistence, and chatService.processMessage — the same code path as authenticated web chat. Dedicated per-platform endpoints route through verifyAndLookupBinding (im.routes.ts:229); the generic endpoint has no equivalent control.
poc_description: 1. Seed a Slack IM binding with a signing secret. 2. Send an unauthenticated POST to /api/im/webhook/<bindingId> with arbitrary text. 3. Observe the backend accept the request, create a chat session, and route the text into chatService.processMessage.
remediation_steps: Require a per-binding authentication secret on the generic webhook endpoint (shared-secret header compared timing-safely, or HMAC over the raw body), validated before imService.handleMessage is invoked. Never allow a binding lookup path that bypasses adapter verifyRequest.
evidence: Local PoC against backend on 127.0.0.1:3001 with seeded Slack binding (signing secret in config): `curl -X POST http://127.0.0.1:3001/api/im/webhook/33333333-3333-3333-3333-333333333333 -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"text":"hello from attacker","user_id":"attacker-1"}'` → request routed to chatService.processMessage; DB shows new chat_sessions row with source='im' created by the unauthenticated request. The signed Slack endpoint rejects signature-less requests, proving the dedicated endpoints enforce verification while the generic one has none.
assumptions: Attacker knows a valid IM binding UUID; endpoint is network-reachable.
counterevidence: Requires knowing the bindingId UUID; route checks is_enabled; generic 500 hides detail. No signature header is expected, so no control exists to bypass — verification is simply absent.
confidence_rationale: Confirmed dynamically against a local instance of the real backend: unauthenticated request accepted and chat session row created in database.
severity_change_conditions: A cheap way to enumerate bindingIds (ID leakage) would lower attack complexity and raise severity to critical.

title: Workflow webhook trigger ignores generated secret — unauthenticated workflow execution
description: The public webhook trigger endpoint `POST /v1/webhook/:webhookId/trigger` never verifies the per-webhook secret. A secret is generated and its hash stored on creation, but the trigger path ignores it entirely, so any caller who knows a webhook ID can execute the workflow with attacker-chosen variables, without any signature or shared secret.
impact: Unauthenticated triggering of tenant workflows with attacker-controlled variables (which become workflow variable values in the V2 plan), including agent and action node execution. Also public status endpoint /v1/webhook/status/:callRecordId leaks execution status and logs without auth.
technical_analysis: src/routes/webhooks.routes.ts:278-320 registers the trigger route with no authenticate preHandler; src/services/webhook.service.ts triggerWebhook (lines ~140-192) validates only existence, isEnabled, and optional IP allowlist. The secretHash generated in createWebhook (webhook.service.ts:75-84) is never read or compared anywhere in the trigger path — grep shows secretHash only set and mapped. No signature, timestamp, or nonce checks exist, so replay is also unrestricted.
poc_description: 1. Run `npx vitest run tests/unit/webhook-trigger-authz.poc.test.ts` in super-agent/backend — it registers the real route plugin under the production /api prefix with mocked prisma/redis/executor and a webhook record carrying a non-null secret_hash. 2. The suite proves: a POST with no secret header returns 200 received:true; a wrong x-webhook-secret header is ignored; identical replays succeed without limit (3 replays = 3 call records created). Equivalently on a live deployment: POST /api/v1/webhook/<id>/trigger with arbitrary variables and no signature headers executes the workflow.
poc_script_code:
```bash
cd super-agent/backend
npx vitest run tests/unit/webhook-trigger-authz.poc.test.ts
# ✓ service layer: triggerWebhook accepts a wrong secret header without complaint
# ✓ route layer: POST with NO secret header returns 200 received:true
# ✓ route layer: identical replay also returns 200 received:true (no replay protection)
#   3 triggers => 3 call records created, 3 executions attempted
```
remediation_steps: When a webhook has a secret_hash, require a signature (e.g. HMAC-SHA256 of the raw body with the secret, compared timing-safely) or a shared-secret header before creating the call record; add timestamp freshness checking.
evidence:
Code trace: webhooks.routes.ts:315 (public trigger route, no preHandler authenticate; registered under /api at routes/index.ts:209); webhook.service.ts:137-186 triggerWebhook checks only existence, isEnabled, optional IP allowlist; secretHash generated at :50-53, stored at :93, mapped at :524 — repo-wide search shows no comparison site; no timestamp/nonce replay protection.

Executable PoC (vitest, real route + service, mocked prisma/redis/executor) at tests/unit/webhook-trigger-authz.poc.test.ts — `npx vitest run` passes 3/3:
- POST /api/v1/webhook/<id>/trigger with NO secret header -> 200 {received:true, callRecordId}
- Request with `x-webhook-secret: totally-wrong-value` -> also accepted
- Identical request replayed 3x -> 200 each time, 3 call records + 3 executions created (no replay protection)
assumptions: A webhook was created with generateSecret=true; attacker knows the webhookId.
counterevidence: Webhook ID is 24 random hex chars (96 bits) — unguessable without leak. IP allowlist applies when configured. Secret verification may be a deliberately deferred feature (secretHash only stored, never read).
confidence_rationale: Executable local PoC: vitest suite registering the real webhooks.routes.ts under the production /api prefix (mocked prisma/redis/executor) shows POST with no secret header returns 200 received:true, wrong secret header is ignored, and identical replays succeed without limit. Only deployment exposure of the URL is inferred.
severity_change_conditions: WebhookId leakage (e.g. via history responses or URLs) would lower complexity and raise severity.

update_history.reason: Added an executable local PoC (vitest test registering the real route file with mocked prisma) proving no-secret and replay acceptance dynamically, strengthening the previously static evidence.
